RESEARCH IDENTITY
Source lineage: Mother II - Part V plus agency boundaries. N4 isolates the science of BCIadjacent sensing, intent as a latent variable, task labels versus natural intention, state
decoding, motor intention, continuous decoding, closed-loop feedback, decoding utility, and
human-controlled interfaces.
CORE RESEARCH QUESTION
When can a decoder support useful closed-loop action without turning task structure, state
correlation, or model confidence into an unjustified claim about human intention?
FLAGSHIP THREE-COUPLING
Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
PROPOSED MOTHER HEURISTIC
IBCI = (Id * Lu * Ha * Cc) / (1 + Ll + Fa + Ao)
Variables: Id = Intent Decodability; Lu = Closed-Loop Utility; Ha = Human Agency; Cc =
Confidence Calibration. Risk denominator: Ll = Label Leakage; Fa = cost-weighted False
Activation; Ao = Agency Override.
EPISTEMIC STATUS
The mother heuristic and all new normalized indices in this architecture are research-design
instruments, not laws of nature.
N4 / MIND - NEURAL INTERFACE AT THE LIMIT
2
ABSTRACT
This volume develops a research architecture for intent-sensitive neural interfaces. It
separates observed neural activity, inferred state, inferred intention, and userauthorized action; treats intention as a latent and revisable construct; and evaluates
closed-loop systems through the coupled dimensions of Intent Decodability, Closed-Loop
Utility, and Human Agency. The proposed mother heuristic IBCI and all chapter-level
indices are design instruments for disciplined comparison, not laws of nature. The
objective is not unrestricted mind reading. The objective is useful assistance under
declared uncertainty, bounded inference, calibrated confidence, reversible control,
traceable authorization, and preserved human agency.
MOTHER-POTENTIAL TEST
If interface performance can improve while intent validity or user control degrades,
intent-decoding science must exist as a standalone mother domain.
SUCCESSOR-READY HANDOFF
Preserve label-generation logic, behavioral references, decoder versions, confidence,
false activations, user corrections, override events, feedback history, privacy and
consent state, and null trials. A successor must be able to reconstruct why an inference
was made, why an action was permitted, and how a user could interrupt or revise it.
DESIGN PROMISE
The book is written as a research instrument. Each chapter separates construct claims
from engineering performance, each major section has a page-scale unit, each Research
Gate can be entered independently, and each Answer Embryo remains provisional,
falsifiable, and capable of mutation.
N4 / MIND - NEURAL INTERFACE AT THE LIMIT
3
HOW TO READ THIS FLAGSHIP
The volume is deliberately modular. Each chapter begins from a narrow construct and
expands through measurement, geometric reasoning, closed-loop control, adversarial
failure analysis, and successor-ready experimental design. The repeated architecture is
intentional: it allows different subfields to be compared without pretending that their
signals, labels, consequences, or user populations are interchangeable.
A page that contains a formula should be read as a design instrument. Terms are
placeholders for operational definitions, units, normalization choices, and validation
procedures. No normalized index in this book should be interpreted as a biological
constant, a clinical threshold, or a regulatory standard. Its purpose is to expose what
must be measured together and what failure modes must remain visible.
The later Research Gates do not summarize the book. They reopen it. Each Gate
specifies a core unknown, a coupling, an instrument, a boundary condition, an evidence
route, a red-team attack, and a successor link. The 33 Answer Embryos then attempt
provisional synthesis. They are designed to be falsified, decomposed, recombined, and
reborn as stronger structures when evidence changes.
Research path = Construct -> Measurement -> Geometry -> Closed loop -> Red
team -> Handoff -> Gate -> Answer Embryo

Closed-Loop Control Torus
user - decoder
feedback loop
A cyclical model of reciprocal adaptation. Decoder output changes feedback; feedback
changes user behavior; user behavior changes future data; future data changes the
decoder. The torus prevents the loop from being described as a one-way sensing
pipeline.
Closed-Loop_Control_Torus = f(evidence, uncertainty, utility, consequence,
reversibility, agency)

CHAPTER 01 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
The Neural Interface Problem
RESEARCH FRAME
C1.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for The Neural Interface Problem. Improvement in
one dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the others. A system may
become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more accurate by
narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result guarantees
that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a joint region
in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority remain
simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in The Neural Interface Problem is not whether a model can
produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition that output is
allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task phase, preparation, attention,
fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental regularity. A useful research
program therefore begins by declaring the inferential target and the level of claim. In
this volume, the target is treated as a latent and revisable construct rather than a
directly observed object. That choice prevents technical success from silently becoming
semantic overreach.
For The Neural Interface Problem, the book adopts a four-layer distinction: observed
signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action. These layers may
correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can be excellent at
identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary intention.
Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external actuation. The
research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and measure what
crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human control remain
visible rather than being averaged away.
For Chapter 1, the working emphasis is the neural interface problem. The section uses
uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt counterfactual control probes while explicitly searching for
state confounding. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 01 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
The Neural Interface Problem
MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C1.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A natural-label protocol for The Neural Interface Problem should avoid the fiction that
intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category. Labels can be intervalvalued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally inferred, externally
constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error model. Instead of
collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the proposed architecture
keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and disagreement explicit. This
allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of the label itself rather than
against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for The Neural Interface Problem includes
discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action severity,
correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These measures should be
reported together because they answer different questions. Accuracy describes
classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration describes whether
confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system can
remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the user must
perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether the user
can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
Measurement for The Neural Interface Problem should preserve provenance from raw
observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of sensor channels,
preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral references,
contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and authorization
state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the additional
structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather than task
classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether performance came
from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or downstream correction.
For Chapter 1, the working emphasis is the neural interface problem. The section uses
control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt longitudinal recalibration while explicitly searching for false activation. If
performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and
correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the
claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 01 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
The Neural Interface Problem
GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C1.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The geometric model for The Neural Interface Problem treats the design space as a field
rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for the target construct, y
represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user control. Regions of high x
and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile. Regions of high y but low
x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the reason claimed. The
preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface bounded by acceptable
uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
A local design instrument for The Neural Interface Problem is defined as C1 = (V * U * A
* K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is task utility, A is agency
retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is cost-weighted false activation,
O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This expression is not proposed
as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that forces numerator gains and
denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame. Different applications may
replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of The Neural Interface Problem should be explored through
perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable point; it is
one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context changes,
sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action increases.
Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system stays
inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into overconfident or
over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
For Chapter 1, the working emphasis is the neural interface problem. The section uses
agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats authorization fidelity as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt behaviorally anchored ground truth while explicitly searching for confidence
inflation. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.
N4 / MIND - NEURAL INTERFACE AT THE LIMIT

CHAPTER 01 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
The Neural Interface Problem
CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C1.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Feedback quality for The Neural Interface Problem should be assessed by more than
task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's intention
easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively more
constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user to
behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it must
not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation is
therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of
alternative action paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in The Neural Interface Problem.
Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the user, the system
is no longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics that generate later
data. Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder adaptation, user
adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without separate ledgers,
apparent learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to person or a gradual
narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can recognize.
Human control in The Neural Interface Problem is modeled as a set of capabilities
rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to withhold action,
correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and interrupt
automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some applications
also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible actuation,
and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control
model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
For Chapter 1, the working emphasis is the neural interface problem. The section uses
false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats agency retention as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt blinded relabeling while explicitly searching for context
collapse. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.

CHAPTER 01 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
The Neural Interface Problem
RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C1.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Failure analysis for The Neural Interface Problem uses consequence-weighted
categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not equivalent
to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for The Neural Interface Problem includes label
permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session transfer,
sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
The red-team question for The Neural Interface Problem is deliberately adversarial: how
could every headline metric improve while the central claim becomes less true? One
pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy while reducing ecological
validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model learns timing, device state, or
environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where user corrections become rarer
because the system acts earlier, not because it understands better. Stress tests must be
designed to expose these possibilities rather than treating them as post hoc caveats.
For Chapter 1, the working emphasis is the neural interface problem. The section uses
leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats closed-loop regret as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt out-of-distribution challenge sets while explicitly searching for automation
creep. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.

CHAPTER 01 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
The Neural Interface Problem
EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF
C1.6 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Design evidence that another team can reproduce, challenge, and inherit.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The experimental program for The Neural Interface Problem should be successor-ready.
Another team must be able to reconstruct not only the model weights but also why a
particular output was interpreted as evidence of intention and why an action was
permitted. The handoff record therefore preserves label-generation logic, behavioral
anchors, decoder versions, confidence calibration, false activations, user corrections,
override events, feedback history, consent state, privacy state, and null trials. This
makes later reinterpretation possible when definitions, standards, or models change.
A staged program for The Neural Interface Problem moves from construct validation to
controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability, longitudinal drift, and
governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by evidence rather than
by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation from intended action
should not advance merely because its benchmark score is high. Conversely, a modest
decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and low correction burden may
deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating limits are legible.
The final success criterion for The Neural Interface Problem is not perfect mind reading.
It is a narrower and more defensible achievement: useful assistance under declared
uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims, reversible control, and preserved
human authority. That criterion is intentionally compatible with partial success. It allows
the science to mature through falsification and refinement rather than forcing every
experiment to imply that intention has been fully captured. The successor question is
always what evidence would justify the next increase in autonomy without shrinking the
user's practical control.
For Chapter 1, the working emphasis is the neural interface problem. The section uses
utility landscape as a visual reasoning aid and treats calibration error as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt human override logs while explicitly searching for agency override. If
performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and
correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the
claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

The geometry of Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding should be explored through
perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable point; it is
one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context changes,
sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action increases.
Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system stays
inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into overconfident or
over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
The geometric model for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding treats the design
space as a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for the target
construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user control.
Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile. Regions
of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the reason
claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface bounded
by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
A local design instrument for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding is defined as C2
= (V * U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is task utility, A
is agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is cost-weighted false
activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This expression is
not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that forces numerator
gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame. Different applications
may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.

accuracy.

CHAPTER 02 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding
CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C2.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Human control in Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding is modeled as a set of
capabilities rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to withhold
action, correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and interrupt
automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some applications
also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible actuation,
and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control
model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
Feedback quality for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding should be assessed by
more than task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's
intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively
more constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user
to behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it
must not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation
is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of
alternative action paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Why Decoding Is Not Yet
Understanding. Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the
user, the system is no longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics
that generate later data. Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder
adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without
separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to
person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can
recognize.
For Chapter 2, the working emphasis is why decoding is not yet understanding. The
section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats override latency
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt latency-aware closed-loop trials while explicitly searching
for automation creep. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C2.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The red-team question for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding is deliberately
adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central claim becomes
less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy while reducing
ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model learns timing, device
state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where user corrections
become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it understands better. Stress
tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather than treating them as post
hoc caveats.
Failure analysis for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding uses consequence-weighted
categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not equivalent
to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding includes label
permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session transfer,
sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
For Chapter 2, the working emphasis is why decoding is not yet understanding. The
section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats false-action severity as
a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt preregistered perturbation tests while explicitly searching
for agency override. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding
EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF
C2.6 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Design evidence that another team can reproduce, challenge, and inherit.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The final success criterion for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding is not perfect
mind reading. It is a narrower and more defensible achievement: useful assistance
under declared uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims, reversible control,
and preserved human authority. That criterion is intentionally compatible with partial
success. It allows the science to mature through falsification and refinement rather than
forcing every experiment to imply that intention has been fully captured. The successor
question is always what evidence would justify the next increase in autonomy without
shrinking the user's practical control.
The experimental program for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding should be
successor-ready. Another team must be able to reconstruct not only the model weights
but also why a particular output was interpreted as evidence of intention and why an
action was permitted. The handoff record therefore preserves label-generation logic,
behavioral anchors, decoder versions, confidence calibration, false activations, user
corrections, override events, feedback history, consent state, privacy state, and null
trials. This makes later reinterpretation possible when definitions, standards, or models
change.
A staged program for Why Decoding Is Not Yet Understanding moves from construct
validation to controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability, longitudinal drift,
and governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by evidence rather
than by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation from intended
action should not advance merely because its benchmark score is high. Conversely, a
modest decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and low correction burden may
deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating limits are legible.
For Chapter 2, the working emphasis is why decoding is not yet understanding. The
section uses utility landscape as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt cross-context validation while explicitly searching for
feedback-induced drift. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 03 / I - WHY INTENT NEEDS ITS OWN SCIENCE
Intent as a Latent Variable
RESEARCH FRAME
C3.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The central problem in Intent as a Latent Variable is not whether a model can produce a
discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition that output is allowed to
support. Neural activity can covary with task phase, preparation, attention, fatigue,
affect, movement, expectation, or environmental regularity. A useful research program
therefore begins by declaring the inferential target and the level of claim. In this
volume, the target is treated as a latent and revisable construct rather than a directly
observed object. That choice prevents technical success from silently becoming
semantic overreach.
For Intent as a Latent Variable, the book adopts a four-layer distinction: observed signal,
inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action. These layers may correlate
strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can be excellent at identifying a
state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary intention. Likewise, a credible
intention estimate does not itself authorize external actuation. The research design
must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and measure what crosses them.
Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human control remain visible rather
than being averaged away.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Intent as a Latent Variable. Improvement in one
dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the others. A system may
become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more accurate by
narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result guarantees
that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a joint region
in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority remain
simultaneously defensible.
For Chapter 3, the working emphasis is intent as a latent variable. The section uses
uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt latency-aware closed-loop trials while explicitly searching
for confidence inflation. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C3.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The minimum measurement set for Intent as a Latent Variable includes discriminative
performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action severity, correction burden,
override latency, and context robustness. These measures should be reported together
because they answer different questions. Accuracy describes classification under a
selected task distribution. Calibration describes whether confidence tracks empirical
reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system can remain safely inactive. Correction
burden estimates how much work the user must perform to keep the interface aligned.
Agency-related measures ask whether the user can still redirect the system when the
model is wrong.
Measurement for Intent as a Latent Variable should preserve provenance from raw
observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of sensor channels,
preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral references,
contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and authorization
state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the additional
structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather than task
classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether performance came
from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or downstream correction.
A natural-label protocol for Intent as a Latent Variable should avoid the fiction that
intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category. Labels can be intervalvalued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally inferred, externally
constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error model. Instead of
collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the proposed architecture
keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and disagreement explicit. This
allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of the label itself rather than
against an artificially perfect annotation.
For Chapter 3, the working emphasis is intent as a latent variable. The section uses
control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt preregistered perturbation tests while explicitly searching for context collapse.
If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and
correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the
claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

drift. This expression is not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic
that forces numerator gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame.
Different applications may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific Program should be
explored through perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a
favorable point; it is one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become
noisier, context changes, sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false
action increases. Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the
system stays inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into
overconfident or over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a
research result.
For Chapter 4, the working emphasis is human-controlled interfaces as a distinct

correction burden as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct

searching for agency override. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the
user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails,
the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being

CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C4.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Feedback quality for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific Program
should be assessed by more than task completion. Researchers should ask whether
feedback makes the user's intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to
predict, or progressively more constrained by the interface. A system can become
efficient by teaching the user to behave like its training distribution. That may be
acceptable in some tools, but it must not be misdescribed as improved access to
unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden,
reversibility, and the preservation of alternative action paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Human-Controlled Interfaces
as a Distinct Scientific Program. Once decoder output influences feedback, and
feedback influences the user, the system is no longer observing a static target. It
participates in the dynamics that generate later data. Training and evaluation must
therefore distinguish decoder adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and
environmental adaptation. Without separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a
transfer of burden from machine to person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior
around what the interface can recognize.
Human control in Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific Program is
modeled as a set of capabilities rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should
be able to withhold action, correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where
practical, and interrupt automation within a time window appropriate to the
consequence. Some applications also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial
assistance, reversible actuation, and irreversible actuation should not share the same
threshold. This layered control model prevents a high-confidence decoder from
becoming an implicit command channel.
For Chapter 4, the working emphasis is human-controlled interfaces as a distinct
scientific program. The section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and
treats override latency as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt behaviorally anchored ground truth while
explicitly searching for feedback-induced drift. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C4.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Failure analysis for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific Program uses
consequence-weighted categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor
suggestion is not equivalent to a false positive that initiates physical actuation,
communication, financial commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore
records both probability and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when
to abstain. Safe null behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should
sometimes choose not to infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or
authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific
Program includes label permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking,
cross-session transfer, sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence
miscalibration, user disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The
purpose is not to make deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the
performance claim survives when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure
envelope defines where the system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and
where it should remain inactive.
The red-team question for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific Program
is deliberately adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central
claim becomes less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy
while reducing ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model
learns timing, device state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where
user corrections become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it
understands better. Stress tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather
than treating them as post hoc caveats.
For Chapter 4, the working emphasis is human-controlled interfaces as a distinct
scientific program. The section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats
false-action severity as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt blinded relabeling while explicitly
searching for selection bias. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the
user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails,
the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being
hidden by aggregate accuracy.

EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF
C4.6 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Design evidence that another team can reproduce, challenge, and inherit.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The experimental program for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific
Program should be successor-ready. Another team must be able to reconstruct not only
the model weights but also why a particular output was interpreted as evidence of
intention and why an action was permitted. The handoff record therefore preserves
label-generation logic, behavioral anchors, decoder versions, confidence calibration,
false activations, user corrections, override events, feedback history, consent state,
privacy state, and null trials. This makes later reinterpretation possible when
definitions, standards, or models change.
A staged program for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific Program
moves from construct validation to controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic
variability, longitudinal drift, and governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should
be gated by evidence rather than by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state
correlation from intended action should not advance merely because its benchmark
score is high. Conversely, a modest decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and
low correction burden may deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating
limits are legible.
The final success criterion for Human-Controlled Interfaces as a Distinct Scientific
Program is not perfect mind reading. It is a narrower and more defensible achievement:
useful assistance under declared uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims,
reversible control, and preserved human authority. That criterion is intentionally
compatible with partial success. It allows the science to mature through falsification and
refinement rather than forcing every experiment to imply that intention has been fully
captured. The successor question is always what evidence would justify the next
increase in autonomy without shrinking the user's practical control.

after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim
becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next

From Observation to Authorization
RESEARCH FRAME
C5.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
For From Observation to Authorization, the book adopts a four-layer distinction:
observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action. These layers
may correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can be excellent at
identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary intention.
Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external actuation. The
research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and measure what
crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human control remain
visible rather than being averaged away.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for From Observation to Authorization.
Improvement in one dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the others.
A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more
accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result
guarantees that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a
joint region in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority
remain simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in From Observation to Authorization is not whether a model can
produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition that output is
allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task phase, preparation, attention,
fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental regularity. A useful research
program therefore begins by declaring the inferential target and the level of claim. In
this volume, the target is treated as a latent and revisable construct rather than a
directly observed object. That choice prevents technical success from silently becoming
semantic overreach.
For Chapter 5, the working emphasis is from observation to authorization. The section
uses uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt behaviorally anchored ground truth while explicitly
searching for automation creep. If performance remains stable after that stressor and
the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it
fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being
hidden by aggregate accuracy.

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C5.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Measurement for From Observation to Authorization should preserve provenance from
raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of sensor channels,
preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral references,
contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and authorization

structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather than task
classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether performance came
from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or downstream correction.
A natural-label protocol for From Observation to Authorization should avoid the fiction
that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category. Labels can be
interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally inferred, externally
constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error model. Instead of
collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the proposed architecture
keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and disagreement explicit. This
allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of the label itself rather than
against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for From Observation to Authorization includes
discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action severity,
correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These measures should be
reported together because they answer different questions. Accuracy describes
classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration describes whether
confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system can
remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the user must
perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether the user
can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.

uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive

veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should

accuracy.

CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C6.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in The Core Iron: Output Is Not
Permission. Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the user,
the system is no longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics that
generate later data. Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder
adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without
separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to
person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can
recognize.
Human control in The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission is modeled as a set of
capabilities rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to withhold
action, correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and interrupt
automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some applications
also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible actuation,
and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control
model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
Feedback quality for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission should be assessed by
more than task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's
intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively
more constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user
to behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it
must not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation
is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of
alternative action paths.
For Chapter 6, the working emphasis is the core iron: output is not permission. The
section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats override latency
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt cross-context validation while explicitly searching for silent
nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C6.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A minimum red-team battery for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission includes label
permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session transfer,
sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
The red-team question for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission is deliberately
adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central claim becomes
less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy while reducing
ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model learns timing, device
state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where user corrections
become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it understands better. Stress
tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather than treating them as post
hoc caveats.
Failure analysis for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission uses consequence-weighted
categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not equivalent
to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
For Chapter 6, the working emphasis is the core iron: output is not permission. The
section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats false-action severity as
a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt null-trial stress testing while explicitly searching for label
leakage. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.

EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF
C6.6 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Design evidence that another team can reproduce, challenge, and inherit.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A staged program for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission moves from construct
validation to controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability, longitudinal drift,
and governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by evidence rather
than by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation from intended
action should not advance merely because its benchmark score is high. Conversely, a
modest decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and low correction burden may
deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating limits are legible.
The final success criterion for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission is not perfect
mind reading. It is a narrower and more defensible achievement: useful assistance
under declared uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims, reversible control,
and preserved human authority. That criterion is intentionally compatible with partial
success. It allows the science to mature through falsification and refinement rather than
forcing every experiment to imply that intention has been fully captured. The successor
question is always what evidence would justify the next increase in autonomy without
shrinking the user's practical control.
The experimental program for The Core Iron: Output Is Not Permission should be
successor-ready. Another team must be able to reconstruct not only the model weights
but also why a particular output was interpreted as evidence of intention and why an
action was permitted. The handoff record therefore preserves label-generation logic,
behavioral anchors, decoder versions, confidence calibration, false activations, user
corrections, override events, feedback history, consent state, privacy state, and null
trials. This makes later reinterpretation possible when definitions, standards, or models
change.
For Chapter 6, the working emphasis is the core iron: output is not permission. The
section uses utility landscape as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt counterfactual control probes while explicitly searching for
state confounding. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates,

RESEARCH FRAME
C7.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and
Mixed Sensing. Improvement in one dimension cannot be treated as proof of
improvement in the others. A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual
regularities, or more accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost
predetermined. Neither result guarantees that natural human intention has been
decoded. The research objective is a joint region in which useful action, evidential
validity, and practical human authority remain simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed Sensing is
not whether a model can produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what
proposition that output is allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task
phase, preparation, attention, fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental
regularity. A useful research program therefore begins by declaring the inferential
target and the level of claim. In this volume, the target is treated as a latent and
revisable construct rather than a directly observed object. That choice prevents
technical success from silently becoming semantic overreach.
For Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed Sensing, the book adopts a
four-layer distinction: observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and
authorized action. These layers may correlate strongly while remaining logically
different. A decoder can be excellent at identifying a state transition and still be weak
evidence for a voluntary intention. Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself
authorize external actuation. The research design must therefore preserve the gaps
between layers and measure what crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty,
consent, and human control remain visible rather than being averaged away.
For Chapter 7, the working emphasis is neural activity, physiological correlates, and
mixed sensing. The section uses uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats
intent-validity margin as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt cross-context validation while explicitly
searching for feedback-induced drift. If performance remains stable after that stressor
and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If
it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than
being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C7.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A natural-label protocol for Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed Sensing
should avoid the fiction that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped
category. Labels can be interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported,
behaviorally inferred, externally constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a
different error model. Instead of collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth
column, the proposed architecture keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision,
and disagreement explicit. This allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty
of the label itself rather than against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed
Sensing includes discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, falseaction severity, correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These
measures should be reported together because they answer different questions.
Accuracy describes classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration
describes whether confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether
the system can remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the
user must perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether
the user can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
Measurement for Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed Sensing should
preserve provenance from raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable
account of sensor channels, preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic,
behavioral references, contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user
correction, and authorization state. This is more demanding than storing a final class
label, but the additional structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns
intention rather than task classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask
whether performance came from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure,
or downstream correction.
For Chapter 7, the working emphasis is neural activity, physiological correlates, and
mixed sensing. The section uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats
context robustness as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt null-trial stress testing while explicitly
searching for selection bias. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the
user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails,
the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being
hidden by aggregate accuracy.

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C7.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The geometric model for Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed Sensing
treats the design space as a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent
evidence for the target construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent
preserved user control. Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet
agency-fragile. Regions of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works,
but not for the reason claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a
feasible surface bounded by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit
authorization.
A local design instrument for Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed
Sensing is defined as C7 = (V * U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct
validity, U is task utility, A is agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage,
F is cost-weighted false activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional
drift. This expression is not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic
that forces numerator gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame.
Different applications may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of Neural Activity, Physiological Correlates, and Mixed Sensing should be
explored through perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a
favorable point; it is one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become
noisier, context changes, sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false
action increases. Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the
system stays inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into
overconfident or over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a
research result.
For Chapter 7, the working emphasis is neural activity, physiological correlates, and
mixed sensing. The section uses agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats
authorization fidelity as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt counterfactual control probes while
explicitly searching for silent nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control model prevents a
high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
Feedback quality for State Versus Intent should be assessed by more than task
completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's intention easier
to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively more constrained by
the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user to behave like its
training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it must not be
misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation is therefore
evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of alternative action
paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in State Versus Intent. Once
decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the user, the system is no
longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics that generate later data.
Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder adaptation, user adaptation,
task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without separate ledgers, apparent
learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to person or a gradual
narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can recognize.
For Chapter 8, the working emphasis is state versus intent. The section uses falseactivation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats override latency as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt out-of-distribution challenge sets while explicitly searching for state
confounding. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C8.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The red-team question for State Versus Intent is deliberately adversarial: how could
every headline metric improve while the central claim becomes less true? One pathway
is task simplification, which can raise accuracy while reducing ecological validity.
Another is contextual leakage, where the model learns timing, device state, or
environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where user corrections become rarer
because the system acts earlier, not because it understands better. Stress tests must be
designed to expose these possibilities rather than treating them as post hoc caveats.
Failure analysis for State Versus Intent uses consequence-weighted categories. A false
positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not equivalent to a false positive
that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial commitment, or clinical
intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability and consequence, and it
asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null behavior is treated as an
active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to infer, not to recommend,
or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for State Versus Intent includes label permutation checks,
temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session transfer, sensor dropout,
adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user disagreement, delayed
correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make deployment impossible. It
is to identify which part of the performance claim survives when convenient structure is
removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the system may be useful, where
it requires supervision, and where it should remain inactive.
For Chapter 8, the working emphasis is state versus intent. The section uses leakage
frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats false-action severity as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt human override logs while explicitly searching for false activation. If
performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and
correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the
claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF

Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical

The final success criterion for State Versus Intent is not perfect mind reading. It is a

human authority. That criterion is intentionally compatible with partial success. It allows
the science to mature through falsification and refinement rather than forcing every

The experimental program for State Versus Intent should be successor-ready. Another
team must be able to reconstruct not only the model weights but also why a particular
output was interpreted as evidence of intention and why an action was permitted. The
handoff record therefore preserves label-generation logic, behavioral anchors, decoder
versions, confidence calibration, false activations, user corrections, override events,
feedback history, consent state, privacy state, and null trials. This makes later
reinterpretation possible when definitions, standards, or models change.

closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability, longitudinal drift, and governancerelevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by evidence rather than by model
novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation from intended action should not
advance merely because its benchmark score is high. Conversely, a modest decoder with
strong calibration, safe abstention, and low correction burden may deserve deeper
closed-loop study because its operating limits are legible.

RESEARCH FRAME
C9.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The central problem in Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation is not
whether a model can produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what
proposition that output is allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task
phase, preparation, attention, fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental
regularity. A useful research program therefore begins by declaring the inferential
target and the level of claim. In this volume, the target is treated as a latent and
revisable construct rather than a directly observed object. That choice prevents
technical success from silently becoming semantic overreach.
For Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation, the book adopts a four-layer
distinction: observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action.
These layers may correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can
be excellent at identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary
intention. Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external
actuation. The research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and
measure what crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human
control remain visible rather than being averaged away.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor
Preparation. Improvement in one dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement
in the others. A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or
more accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither
result guarantees that natural human intention has been decoded. The research
objective is a joint region in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human
authority remain simultaneously defensible.
For Chapter 9, the working emphasis is attention, arousal, readiness, and motor
preparation. The section uses uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats
intent-validity margin as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt out-of-distribution challenge sets while
explicitly searching for silent nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.
