MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C9.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The minimum measurement set for Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor
Preparation includes discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, falseaction severity, correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These
measures should be reported together because they answer different questions.
Accuracy describes classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration
describes whether confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether
the system can remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the
user must perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether
the user can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
Measurement for Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation should preserve
provenance from raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of
sensor channels, preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral
references, contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and
authorization state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the
additional structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather
than task classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether
performance came from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or
downstream correction.
A natural-label protocol for Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation should
avoid the fiction that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category.
Labels can be interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally
inferred, externally constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error
model. Instead of collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the
proposed architecture keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and
disagreement explicit. This allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of
the label itself rather than against an artificially perfect annotation.
For Chapter 9, the working emphasis is attention, arousal, readiness, and motor
preparation. The section uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context
robustness as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A
decisive experiment should attempt human override logs while explicitly searching for
label leakage. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C9.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A local design instrument for Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation is
defined as C9 = (V * U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is
task utility, A is agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is costweighted false activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This
expression is not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that
forces numerator gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame.
Different applications may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation should be
explored through perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a
favorable point; it is one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become
noisier, context changes, sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false
action increases. Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the
system stays inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into
overconfident or over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a
research result.
The geometric model for Attention, Arousal, Readiness, and Motor Preparation treats
the design space as a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence
for the target construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user
control. Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile.
Regions of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the
reason claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface
bounded by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
For Chapter 9, the working emphasis is attention, arousal, readiness, and motor
preparation. The section uses agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats
authorization fidelity as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt latency-aware closed-loop trials while
explicitly searching for state confounding. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C10.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +

Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical

Failure analysis for Task Structure and Experimental Contamination uses consequenceweighted categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not
equivalent to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for Task Structure and Experimental Contamination
includes label permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session
transfer, sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
The red-team question for Task Structure and Experimental Contamination is
deliberately adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central
claim becomes less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy
while reducing ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model
learns timing, device state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where
user corrections become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it
understands better. Stress tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather
than treating them as post hoc caveats.

EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF
C10.6 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Design evidence that another team can reproduce, challenge, and inherit.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The experimental program for Task Structure and Experimental Contamination should
be successor-ready. Another team must be able to reconstruct not only the model
weights but also why a particular output was interpreted as evidence of intention and
why an action was permitted. The handoff record therefore preserves label-generation
logic, behavioral anchors, decoder versions, confidence calibration, false activations,
user corrections, override events, feedback history, consent state, privacy state, and null
trials. This makes later reinterpretation possible when definitions, standards, or models
change.
A staged program for Task Structure and Experimental Contamination moves from
construct validation to controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability,
longitudinal drift, and governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by
evidence rather than by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation
from intended action should not advance merely because its benchmark score is high.
Conversely, a modest decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and low
correction burden may deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating limits
are legible.
The final success criterion for Task Structure and Experimental Contamination is not
perfect mind reading. It is a narrower and more defensible achievement: useful
assistance under declared uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims,
reversible control, and preserved human authority. That criterion is intentionally
compatible with partial success. It allows the science to mature through falsification and
refinement rather than forcing every experiment to imply that intention has been fully
captured. The successor question is always what evidence would justify the next
increase in autonomy without shrinking the user's practical control.

CHAPTER 11 / II - SIGNALS, STATES, AND THE PROBLEM OF INFERENCE
Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates
RESEARCH FRAME
C11.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
For Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates, the book adopts a four-layer distinction:
observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action. These layers
may correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can be excellent at
identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary intention.
Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external actuation. The
research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and measure what
crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human control remain
visible rather than being averaged away.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates.
Improvement in one dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the others.
A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more
accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result
guarantees that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a
joint region in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority
remain simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates is not whether a
model can produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition that
output is allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task phase, preparation,
attention, fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental regularity. A useful
research program therefore begins by declaring the inferential target and the level of
claim. In this volume, the target is treated as a latent and revisable construct rather
than a directly observed object. That choice prevents technical success from silently
becoming semantic overreach.
For Chapter 11, the working emphasis is behavioral proxies and hidden correlates. The
section uses uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt counterfactual control probes while explicitly searching for
state confounding. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 11 / II - SIGNALS, STATES, AND THE PROBLEM OF INFERENCE
Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates
MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C11.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Measurement for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates should preserve provenance
from raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of sensor
channels, preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral
references, contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and
authorization state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the
additional structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather
than task classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether
performance came from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or
downstream correction.
A natural-label protocol for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates should avoid the
fiction that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category. Labels can be
interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally inferred, externally
constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error model. Instead of
collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the proposed architecture
keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and disagreement explicit. This
allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of the label itself rather than
against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates includes
discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action severity,
correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These measures should be
reported together because they answer different questions. Accuracy describes
classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration describes whether
confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system can
remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the user must
perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether the user
can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
For Chapter 11, the working emphasis is behavioral proxies and hidden correlates. The
section uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt longitudinal recalibration while explicitly searching for false
activation. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C11.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The geometry of Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates should be explored through
perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable point; it is
one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context changes,
sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action increases.
Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system stays
inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into overconfident or
over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
The geometric model for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates treats the design
space as a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for the target
construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user control.
Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile. Regions
of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the reason
claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface bounded
by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
A local design instrument for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates is defined as
C11 = (V * U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is task
utility, A is agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is costweighted false activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This
expression is not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that
forces numerator gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame.
Different applications may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
For Chapter 11, the working emphasis is behavioral proxies and hidden correlates. The
section uses agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats authorization fidelity as
a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt behaviorally anchored ground truth while explicitly
searching for confidence inflation. If performance remains stable after that stressor and
the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it
fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being
hidden by aggregate accuracy.

Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates
CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C11.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Human control in Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates is modeled as a set of
capabilities rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to withhold
action, correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and interrupt
automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some applications
also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible actuation,
and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control
model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
Feedback quality for Behavioral Proxies and Hidden Correlates should be assessed by
more than task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's
intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively
more constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user
to behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it
must not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation
is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of
alternative action paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Behavioral Proxies and Hidden
Correlates. Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the user,
the system is no longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics that
generate later data. Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder
adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without
separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to
person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can
recognize.
For Chapter 11, the working emphasis is behavioral proxies and hidden correlates. The
section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats agency retention
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt blinded relabeling while explicitly searching for context
collapse. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.

disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
The red-team question for The Ontology of Intent in Neurotechnology is deliberately
adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central claim becomes
less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy while reducing
ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model learns timing, device
state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where user corrections
become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it understands better. Stress
tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather than treating them as post
hoc caveats.
Failure analysis for The Ontology of Intent in Neurotechnology uses consequenceweighted categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not
equivalent to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
For Chapter 12, the working emphasis is the ontology of intent in neurotechnology. The
section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats false-action severity as
a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt preregistered perturbation tests while explicitly searching
for agency override. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical

The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Labels in Scripted Trials. Improvement in one
dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the others. A system may
become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more accurate by
narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result guarantees
that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a joint region
in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority remain
simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in Labels in Scripted Trials is not whether a model can produce a
discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition that output is allowed to
support. Neural activity can covary with task phase, preparation, attention, fatigue,
affect, movement, expectation, or environmental regularity. A useful research program
therefore begins by declaring the inferential target and the level of claim. In this
volume, the target is treated as a latent and revisable construct rather than a directly
observed object. That choice prevents technical success from silently becoming
semantic overreach.
For Labels in Scripted Trials, the book adopts a four-layer distinction: observed signal,
inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action. These layers may correlate
strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can be excellent at identifying a
state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary intention. Likewise, a credible
intention estimate does not itself authorize external actuation. The research design
must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and measure what crosses them.
Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human control remain visible rather
than being averaged away.

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C13.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A natural-label protocol for Labels in Scripted Trials should avoid the fiction that
intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category. Labels can be intervalvalued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally inferred, externally
constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error model. Instead of
collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the proposed architecture
keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and disagreement explicit. This
allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of the label itself rather than
against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for Labels in Scripted Trials includes discriminative
performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action severity, correction burden,
override latency, and context robustness. These measures should be reported together
because they answer different questions. Accuracy describes classification under a
selected task distribution. Calibration describes whether confidence tracks empirical
reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system can remain safely inactive. Correction
burden estimates how much work the user must perform to keep the interface aligned.
Agency-related measures ask whether the user can still redirect the system when the
model is wrong.
Measurement for Labels in Scripted Trials should preserve provenance from raw
observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of sensor channels,
preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral references,
contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and authorization
state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the additional
structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather than task
classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether performance came
from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or downstream correction.
For Chapter 13, the working emphasis is labels in scripted trials. The section uses
control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt preregistered perturbation tests while explicitly searching for context collapse.
If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and
correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the
claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C13.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The geometric model for Labels in Scripted Trials treats the design space as a field
rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for the target construct, y
represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user control. Regions of high x
and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile. Regions of high y but low
x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the reason claimed. The
preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface bounded by acceptable
uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
A local design instrument for Labels in Scripted Trials is defined as C13 = (V * U * A *
K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is task utility, A is agency
retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is cost-weighted false activation,
O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This expression is not proposed
as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that forces numerator gains and
denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame. Different applications may
replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of Labels in Scripted Trials should be explored through perturbation. A
trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable point; it is one whose
trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context changes, sensor
quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action increases. Mapping those
trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system stays inside a humancontrolled operating region and where it exits into overconfident or over-automated
behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
For Chapter 13, the working emphasis is labels in scripted trials. The section uses
agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats authorization fidelity as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt cross-context validation while explicitly searching for automation creep. If

CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C13.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Feedback quality for Labels in Scripted Trials should be assessed by more than task
completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's intention easier
to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively more constrained by
the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user to behave like its
training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it must not be
misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation is therefore
evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of alternative action
paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Labels in Scripted Trials. Once
decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the user, the system is no
longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics that generate later data.
Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder adaptation, user adaptation,
task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without separate ledgers, apparent
learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to person or a gradual
narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can recognize.
Human control in Labels in Scripted Trials is modeled as a set of capabilities rather than
a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to withhold action, correct action,
reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and interrupt automation within a
time window appropriate to the consequence. Some applications also require graded
authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible actuation, and irreversible
actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control model prevents a
high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
For Chapter 13, the working emphasis is labels in scripted trials. The section uses falseactivation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats agency retention as a companion
measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive experiment should
attempt null-trial stress testing while explicitly searching for agency override. If
performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical veto and
correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the
claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 14 / III - L ABEL CONSTRUCTION AND NATURAL INTENTION
Natural Labels Outside the Lab
EXPERIMENTAL PROGRAM AND SUCCESSOR HANDOFF
C14.6 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Design evidence that another team can reproduce, challenge, and inherit.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The final success criterion for Natural Labels Outside the Lab is not perfect mind
reading. It is a narrower and more defensible achievement: useful assistance under
declared uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims, reversible control, and
preserved human authority. That criterion is intentionally compatible with partial
success. It allows the science to mature through falsification and refinement rather than
forcing every experiment to imply that intention has been fully captured. The successor
question is always what evidence would justify the next increase in autonomy without
shrinking the user's practical control.
The experimental program for Natural Labels Outside the Lab should be successorready. Another team must be able to reconstruct not only the model weights but also
why a particular output was interpreted as evidence of intention and why an action was
permitted. The handoff record therefore preserves label-generation logic, behavioral
anchors, decoder versions, confidence calibration, false activations, user corrections,
override events, feedback history, consent state, privacy state, and null trials. This
makes later reinterpretation possible when definitions, standards, or models change.
A staged program for Natural Labels Outside the Lab moves from construct validation
to controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability, longitudinal drift, and
governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by evidence rather than
by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation from intended action
should not advance merely because its benchmark score is high. Conversely, a modest
decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and low correction burden may
deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating limits are legible.
For Chapter 14, the working emphasis is natural labels outside the lab. The section uses
utility landscape as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity margin as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt out-of-distribution challenge sets while explicitly searching
for silent nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 15 / III - L ABEL CONSTRUCTION AND NATURAL INTENTION
Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous
Labels
RESEARCH FRAME
C15.1 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The central problem in Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels is not whether
a model can produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition
that output is allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task phase,
preparation, attention, fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental
regularity. A useful research program therefore begins by declaring the inferential
target and the level of claim. In this volume, the target is treated as a latent and
revisable construct rather than a directly observed object. That choice prevents
technical success from silently becoming semantic overreach.
For Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels, the book adopts a four-layer
distinction: observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action.
These layers may correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can
be excellent at identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary
intention. Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external
actuation. The research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and
measure what crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human
control remain visible rather than being averaged away.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous
Labels. Improvement in one dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the
others. A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more
accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result
guarantees that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a
joint region in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority
remain simultaneously defensible.
For Chapter 15, the working emphasis is weak labels, soft labels, and ambiguous labels.
The section uses uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats intent-validity
margin as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A
decisive experiment should attempt behaviorally anchored ground truth while explicitly
searching for automation creep. If performance remains stable after that stressor and
the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it
fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being
hidden by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 15 / III - L ABEL CONSTRUCTION AND NATURAL INTENTION
Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C15.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The minimum measurement set for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels
includes discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action
severity, correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These measures
should be reported together because they answer different questions. Accuracy
describes classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration describes
whether confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system
can remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the user must
perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether the user
can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
Measurement for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels should preserve
provenance from raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of
sensor channels, preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral
references, contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and
authorization state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the
additional structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather
than task classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether
performance came from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or
downstream correction.
A natural-label protocol for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels should
avoid the fiction that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category.
Labels can be interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally
inferred, externally constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error
model. Instead of collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the
proposed architecture keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and
disagreement explicit. This allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of
the label itself rather than against an artificially perfect annotation.
For Chapter 15, the working emphasis is weak labels, soft labels, and ambiguous labels.
The section uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as
a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt blinded relabeling while explicitly searching for agency
override. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.

CHAPTER 15 / III - L ABEL CONSTRUCTION AND NATURAL INTENTION
Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C15.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A local design instrument for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels is
defined as C15 = (V * U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is
task utility, A is agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is costweighted false activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This
expression is not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that
forces numerator gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame.
Different applications may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels should be explored
through perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable
point; it is one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context
changes, sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action
increases. Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system
stays inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into overconfident
or over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
The geometric model for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels treats the
design space as a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for
the target construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user
control. Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile.
Regions of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the
reason claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface
bounded by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
For Chapter 15, the working emphasis is weak labels, soft labels, and ambiguous labels.
The section uses agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats authorization
fidelity as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A
decisive experiment should attempt out-of-distribution challenge sets while explicitly
searching for feedback-induced drift. If performance remains stable after that stressor
and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If
it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than
being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 15 / III - L ABEL CONSTRUCTION AND NATURAL INTENTION
Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous
Labels
CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C15.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and
Ambiguous Labels. Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences
the user, the system is no longer observing a static target. It participates in the
dynamics that generate later data. Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish
decoder adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental adaptation.
Without separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a transfer of burden from
machine to person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior around what the interface
can recognize.
Human control in Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels is modeled as a set
of capabilities rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to
withhold action, correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and
interrupt automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some
applications also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible
actuation, and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered
control model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command
channel.
Feedback quality for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels should be
assessed by more than task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback
makes the user's intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or
progressively more constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by
teaching the user to behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in
some tools, but it must not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained
intention. Co-adaptation is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and
the preservation of alternative action paths.
For Chapter 15, the working emphasis is weak labels, soft labels, and ambiguous labels.
The section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats agency
retention as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A
decisive experiment should attempt human override logs while explicitly searching for
selection bias. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C15.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A minimum red-team battery for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels
includes label permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session
transfer, sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
The red-team question for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels is
deliberately adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central
claim becomes less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy
while reducing ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model
learns timing, device state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where
user corrections become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it
understands better. Stress tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather
than treating them as post hoc caveats.
Failure analysis for Weak Labels, Soft Labels, and Ambiguous Labels uses consequenceweighted categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not
equivalent to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
For Chapter 15, the working emphasis is weak labels, soft labels, and ambiguous labels.
The section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats closed-loop regret
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt latency-aware closed-loop trials while explicitly searching
for silent nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

A staged program for Label Leakage and Shortcut Learning moves from construct
validation to controlled closed-loop use, then to naturalistic variability, longitudinal drift,
and governance-relevant stress tests. Progression should be gated by evidence rather
than by model novelty. A system that cannot separate state correlation from intended
action should not advance merely because its benchmark score is high. Conversely, a
modest decoder with strong calibration, safe abstention, and low correction burden may
deserve deeper closed-loop study because its operating limits are legible.
The final success criterion for Label Leakage and Shortcut Learning is not perfect mind
reading. It is a narrower and more defensible achievement: useful assistance under
declared uncertainty, with traceable evidence, bounded claims, reversible control, and
preserved human authority. That criterion is intentionally compatible with partial
success. It allows the science to mature through falsification and refinement rather than
forcing every experiment to imply that intention has been fully captured. The successor
question is always what evidence would justify the next increase in autonomy without
shrinking the user's practical control.

as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive

Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical

For Ecological Validity in Intent Studies, the book adopts a four-layer distinction:
observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action. These layers
may correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can be excellent at
identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary intention.
Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external actuation. The
research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and measure what
crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human control remain
visible rather than being averaged away.
The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies.
Improvement in one dimension cannot be treated as proof of improvement in the others.
A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or more
accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither result
guarantees that natural human intention has been decoded. The research objective is a
joint region in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human authority
remain simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in Ecological Validity in Intent Studies is not whether a model can
produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition that output is
allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task phase, preparation, attention,
fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental regularity. A useful research
program therefore begins by declaring the inferential target and the level of claim. In
this volume, the target is treated as a latent and revisable construct rather than a
directly observed object. That choice prevents technical success from silently becoming
semantic overreach.

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C17.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Measurement for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies should preserve provenance from
raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of sensor channels,
preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral references,
contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and authorization
state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the additional
structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather than task
classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether performance came
from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or downstream correction.
A natural-label protocol for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies should avoid the fiction
that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category. Labels can be
interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally inferred, externally
constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error model. Instead of
collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the proposed architecture
keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and disagreement explicit. This
allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of the label itself rather than
against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies includes
discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action severity,
correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These measures should be
reported together because they answer different questions. Accuracy describes
classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration describes whether
confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system can
remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the user must
perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether the user
can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
For Chapter 17, the working emphasis is ecological validity in intent studies. The
section uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context robustness as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt null-trial stress testing while explicitly searching for
selection bias. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C17.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The geometry of Ecological Validity in Intent Studies should be explored through
perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable point; it is
one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context changes,
sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action increases.
Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system stays
inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into overconfident or
over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
The geometric model for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies treats the design space as
a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for the target
construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user control.
Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile. Regions
of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the reason
claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface bounded
by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
A local design instrument for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies is defined as C17 = (V
* U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is task utility, A is
agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is cost-weighted false
activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This expression is
not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that forces numerator
gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame. Different applications
may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
For Chapter 17, the working emphasis is ecological validity in intent studies. The
section uses agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats authorization fidelity as
a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt counterfactual control probes while explicitly searching for
silent nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user
retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the
failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden
by aggregate accuracy.

CHAPTER 17 / III - L ABEL CONSTRUCTION AND NATURAL INTENTION
Ecological Validity in Intent Studies
CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C17.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Human control in Ecological Validity in Intent Studies is modeled as a set of capabilities
rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to withhold action,
correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and interrupt
automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some applications
also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible actuation,
and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered control
model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command channel.
Feedback quality for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies should be assessed by more
than task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback makes the user's
intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or progressively
more constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by teaching the user
to behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in some tools, but it
must not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained intention. Co-adaptation
is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and the preservation of
alternative action paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Ecological Validity in Intent
Studies. Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback influences the user, the
system is no longer observing a static target. It participates in the dynamics that
generate later data. Training and evaluation must therefore distinguish decoder
adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental adaptation. Without
separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a transfer of burden from machine to
person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior around what the interface can
recognize.
For Chapter 17, the working emphasis is ecological validity in intent studies. The
section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats agency retention
as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive
experiment should attempt longitudinal recalibration while explicitly searching for label
leakage. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains practical
veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure should
narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by aggregate
accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C17.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +

Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical

The red-team question for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies is deliberately
adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central claim becomes
less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy while reducing
ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model learns timing, device
state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where user corrections
become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it understands better. Stress
tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather than treating them as post
hoc caveats.
Failure analysis for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies uses consequence-weighted
categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not equivalent
to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for Ecological Validity in Intent Studies includes label
permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session transfer,
sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.

section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats closed-loop regret as a
companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A decisive

searching for state confounding. If performance remains stable after that stressor and

Define the construct before optimizing the decoder.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical

The flagship three-coupling - Intent Decodability x Closed-Loop Utility x Human Agency
- provides the organizing constraint for Human Meaning Versus Experimental

in the others. A system may become more useful by exploiting contextual regularities, or
more accurate by narrowing the task until the label is almost predetermined. Neither
result guarantees that natural human intention has been decoded. The research
objective is a joint region in which useful action, evidential validity, and practical human
authority remain simultaneously defensible.
The central problem in Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation is not whether
a model can produce a discriminative output. The harder question is what proposition
that output is allowed to support. Neural activity can covary with task phase,
preparation, attention, fatigue, affect, movement, expectation, or environmental
regularity. A useful research program therefore begins by declaring the inferential
target and the level of claim. In this volume, the target is treated as a latent and
revisable construct rather than a directly observed object. That choice prevents
technical success from silently becoming semantic overreach.
For Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation, the book adopts a four-layer
distinction: observed signal, inferred state, candidate intention, and authorized action.
These layers may correlate strongly while remaining logically different. A decoder can
be excellent at identifying a state transition and still be weak evidence for a voluntary
intention. Likewise, a credible intention estimate does not itself authorize external
actuation. The research design must therefore preserve the gaps between layers and
measure what crosses them. Those gaps are where uncertainty, consent, and human
control remain visible rather than being averaged away.

annotation. The section uses uncertainty cone as a visual reasoning aid and treats
intent-validity margin as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt out-of-distribution challenge sets while
explicitly searching for silent nonstationarity. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

MEASUREMENT AND LABEL ARCHITECTURE
C19.2 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Separate observation, annotation, inference, and authorization.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
A natural-label protocol for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation should
avoid the fiction that intention is always available as a crisp timestamped category.
Labels can be interval-valued, probabilistic, delayed, self-reported, behaviorally
inferred, externally constrained, or jointly adjudicated. Each source has a different error
model. Instead of collapsing these sources into a single ground-truth column, the
proposed architecture keeps label source, confidence, temporal precision, and
disagreement explicit. This allows the model to be evaluated against the uncertainty of
the label itself rather than against an artificially perfect annotation.
The minimum measurement set for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation
includes discriminative performance, calibration, abstention behavior, false-action
severity, correction burden, override latency, and context robustness. These measures
should be reported together because they answer different questions. Accuracy
describes classification under a selected task distribution. Calibration describes
whether confidence tracks empirical reliability. Abstention reveals whether the system
can remain safely inactive. Correction burden estimates how much work the user must
perform to keep the interface aligned. Agency-related measures ask whether the user
can still redirect the system when the model is wrong.
Measurement for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation should preserve
provenance from raw observation to action. Every trial needs a traceable account of
sensor channels, preprocessing, temporal windows, label-generation logic, behavioral
references, contextual variables, decoder version, uncertainty, user correction, and
authorization state. This is more demanding than storing a final class label, but the
additional structure is necessary when the scientific claim concerns intention rather
than task classification. Provenance enables later investigators to ask whether
performance came from neural content, timing cues, environmental structure, or
downstream correction.
For Chapter 19, the working emphasis is human meaning versus experimental
annotation. The section uses control torus as a visual reasoning aid and treats context
robustness as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct validity. A
decisive experiment should attempt human override logs while explicitly searching for
label leakage. If performance remains stable after that stressor and the user retains
practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it fails, the failure
should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being hidden by
aggregate accuracy.

GEOMETRY AND DESIGN INSTRUMENT
C19.3 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Use geometry to expose tradeoffs that a single accuracy number hides.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
The geometric model for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation treats the
design space as a field rather than a scalar leaderboard. Let x represent evidence for
the target construct, y represent closed-loop utility, and z represent preserved user
control. Regions of high x and y but low z are operationally attractive yet agency-fragile.
Regions of high y but low x indicate shortcut utility: the interface works, but not for the
reason claimed. The preferred region is not a single optimum; it is a feasible surface
bounded by acceptable uncertainty, reversible action, and explicit authorization.
A local design instrument for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation is
defined as C19 = (V * U * A * K) / (1 + L + F + O + D), where V is construct validity, U is
task utility, A is agency retention, K is calibration quality, L is label leakage, F is costweighted false activation, O is unauthorized override, and D is distributional drift. This
expression is not proposed as a law of nature. It is a research-design heuristic that
forces numerator gains and denominator risks to be discussed in the same frame.
Different applications may replace, rescale, or remove terms after empirical validation.
The geometry of Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation should be explored
through perturbation. A trustworthy model is not merely one that sits at a favorable
point; it is one whose trajectory remains acceptable when labels become noisier, context
changes, sensor quality falls, user behavior adapts, or the cost of a false action
increases. Mapping those trajectories produces a practical boundary: where the system
stays inside a human-controlled operating region and where it exits into overconfident
or over-automated behavior. The shape of that boundary is itself a research result.
For Chapter 19, the working emphasis is human meaning versus experimental
annotation. The section uses agency surface as a visual reasoning aid and treats
authorization fidelity as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt latency-aware closed-loop trials while
explicitly searching for state confounding. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

CLOSED-LOOP AND HUMAN CONTROL
C19.4 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Treat feedback as an intervention that changes both person and model.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Feedback quality for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation should be
assessed by more than task completion. Researchers should ask whether feedback
makes the user's intention easier to express, merely easier for the model to predict, or
progressively more constrained by the interface. A system can become efficient by
teaching the user to behave like its training distribution. That may be acceptable in
some tools, but it must not be misdescribed as improved access to unconstrained
intention. Co-adaptation is therefore evaluated for symmetry, burden, reversibility, and
the preservation of alternative action paths.
Closed-loop evaluation changes the epistemic problem in Human Meaning Versus
Experimental Annotation. Once decoder output influences feedback, and feedback
influences the user, the system is no longer observing a static target. It participates in
the dynamics that generate later data. Training and evaluation must therefore
distinguish decoder adaptation, user adaptation, task adaptation, and environmental
adaptation. Without separate ledgers, apparent learning can conceal a transfer of
burden from machine to person or a gradual narrowing of user behavior around what
the interface can recognize.
Human control in Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation is modeled as a set
of capabilities rather than a ceremonial approval step. The user should be able to
withhold action, correct action, reverse action, inspect uncertainty where practical, and
interrupt automation within a time window appropriate to the consequence. Some
applications also require graded authorization: suggestion, partial assistance, reversible
actuation, and irreversible actuation should not share the same threshold. This layered
control model prevents a high-confidence decoder from becoming an implicit command
channel.
For Chapter 19, the working emphasis is human meaning versus experimental
annotation. The section uses false-activation basin as a visual reasoning aid and treats
agency retention as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt preregistered perturbation tests while
explicitly searching for false activation. If performance remains stable after that
stressor and the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes
stronger. If it fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design
rather than being hidden by aggregate accuracy.

RED TEAM AND FAILURE ENVELOPE
C19.5 = (Evidence * Utility * Agency * Calibration) / (1 + Leakage +
FalseAction + Override + Drift)
Search for cases where performance rises while validity or agency falls.
Research-design instrument. Terms are placeholders for operational definitions and empirical
validation, not physical constants.
Failure analysis for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation uses consequenceweighted categories. A false positive that triggers a reversible cursor suggestion is not
equivalent to a false positive that initiates physical actuation, communication, financial
commitment, or clinical intervention. The evaluation therefore records both probability
and consequence, and it asks whether the system knows when to abstain. Safe null
behavior is treated as an active capability: the interface should sometimes choose not to
infer, not to recommend, or not to act when uncertainty or authorization is insufficient.
A minimum red-team battery for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation
includes label permutation checks, temporal scrambling, context masking, cross-session
transfer, sensor dropout, adversarially similar states, confidence miscalibration, user
disagreement, delayed correction, and forced null trials. The purpose is not to make
deployment impossible. It is to identify which part of the performance claim survives
when convenient structure is removed. The resulting failure envelope defines where the
system may be useful, where it requires supervision, and where it should remain
inactive.
The red-team question for Human Meaning Versus Experimental Annotation is
deliberately adversarial: how could every headline metric improve while the central
claim becomes less true? One pathway is task simplification, which can raise accuracy
while reducing ecological validity. Another is contextual leakage, where the model
learns timing, device state, or environmental cues. A third is automation creep, where
user corrections become rarer because the system acts earlier, not because it
understands better. Stress tests must be designed to expose these possibilities rather
than treating them as post hoc caveats.
For Chapter 19, the working emphasis is human meaning versus experimental
annotation. The section uses leakage frontier as a visual reasoning aid and treats
closed-loop regret as a companion measure rather than a replacement for construct
validity. A decisive experiment should attempt cross-context validation while explicitly
searching for confidence inflation. If performance remains stable after that stressor and
the user retains practical veto and correction power, the claim becomes stronger. If it
fails, the failure should narrow the claim and improve the next design rather than being
hidden by aggregate accuracy.
